Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 35
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: UX Designer
  trauma_type: Life-threatening illness
  pcl5: 73

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Medical Cues: Hospitals/ Ambulances/ Physical Examinations, Avoid Thinking: Thinking about the event, Avoid Physical Stress: Situations that put my body under stress
  Threat: Threat in Delays: When something takes longer than expected I assume something bad is happening, Cannot Trust Safety: Even when others tell me I am safe I find it impossible to believe it, Body on Alert: My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger
  Negative Appraisals: Defective Self: There is something wrong with me as a person, Emotional Numbness: I feel dead inside, Weakness Belief: I am a weak person

Vignette:
When the diagnosis came, it did not arrive with drama. There was no emergency room, no collapse in the street. It arrived in a doctor’s office on a Tuesday afternoon, delivered in the careful, measured tone of a physician who had said these words many times before. The patient, a 35-year-old UX designer named Minh, sat in the examination room and heard that a mass had been found in his abdomen, that further testing was needed, that the word “cancer” was being used provisionally. He remembered the way the fluorescent lights hummed, the faint smell of antiseptic, the way the doctor’s mouth kept moving even after the words stopped making sense. What followed were weeks of scans, biopsies, consultations, and a surgery that ultimately removed the tumor successfully. But by then, something else had already taken root.

In the months afterward, Minh found himself avoiding anything that reminded him of that period. He changed his route to work to avoid the hospital where he had been treated. When an ambulance passed on the street, he would turn his head away, his jaw tightening. He stopped scheduling his annual physical, then his biannual blood work. When his wife suggested they watch a medical drama, he felt his chest constrict and told her he wasn’t in the mood. He did not tell her why. He did not tell anyone. He had come to believe, quietly and without ever saying it aloud, that there was something fundamentally wrong with him as a person—that the illness had not been a random biological event but a sign of an inner defect, a weakness that others could not see but that he felt in every bone. He began to feel dead inside, as though a layer of glass had been placed between him and the rest of the world. He could watch his wife laugh, his colleagues joke, his friends plan vacations, and feel nothing. He was certain that he was a weak person, that other people would have handled this better, that his inability to move past it proved something shameful about his character.

His body remained on alert. His shoulders were perpetually hunched, his jaw clenched. He woke several times a night, his heart pounding, unsure what had startled him. At work, where he designed user interfaces for a health-tech company, he found himself unable to tolerate the long loading screens during software testing. When a prototype took more than a few seconds to render, his mind would race: something is wrong, something is breaking, something bad is happening. He knew this was irrational—a delayed render was not a medical emergency—but the feeling did not respond to reason. He had also stopped going to the gym, which he had once enjoyed. Any situation that put his body under stress—a steep hill on his walk home, a heavy box he had to carry—now felt dangerous. He could not explain why. He only knew that when his heart rate rose, he felt as though he were back in that examination room, waiting for the doctor to return with results.

His wife began to notice. She asked him why he seemed distant, why he flinched when she touched his shoulder unexpectedly. He told her he was just tired. He did not tell her that even when she held him at night and whispered that everything was fine, he found it impossible to believe her. He did not tell her that he had started to feel like a stranger in his own life, that the man she had married—the one who used to laugh easily, who planned weekend hikes, who was not afraid of his own body—had been replaced by someone hollow and watchful. The consequence of his avoidance was not dramatic; it was a slow erosion. He stopped initiating plans with friends. He stopped talking about his work. He stopped being present. The space between him and his wife grew wider by the week, filled with things he would not say.

What finally brought him to seek help was not a crisis, but a quiet moment of recognition. He was sitting at his desk, staring at a screen, and realized he could not remember the last time he had felt anything other than dread. He was tired of being afraid of his own heartbeat. He was tired of feeling like a ghost. He came to the clinic not because he believed he could be fixed, but because he was desperate enough to hope that maybe, somewhere beneath the numbness, there was still something worth reaching for.
